headline: Power-cost hardship debated as Auckland transport overhaul passes Parliament
summary: Household energy costs and the Government’s response to hardship were among the sharpest exchanges in Parliament, alongside disputes over jobs, workplace protections and energy policy. MPs also passed legislation changing Auckland’s transport governance, while approving a first reading of expanded Serious Fraud Office powers and beginning the final-stage debate on anti-money-laundering reforms. The sitting ended with that debate unfinished, and Parliament adjourned until 12 May.

topicSummaries.topic: MPs Clash Over Electricity Costs and Energy Hardship
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Electricity bills and the ability to keep homes warm directly affect household budgets, health and wellbeing.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Scott Willis challenged Energy Minister Simeon Brown over rising power bills, energy hardship and cuts to community and efficiency programmes, citing 200,000 households unable to keep their homes adequately warm in 2025. Brown acknowledged high electricity prices but attributed increases to factors including earlier inflation, declining gas supply and previous policy decisions; he pointed to the winter energy payment, increased generation and lower wholesale forward prices as parts of the response. In a separate exchange, Labour’s Megan Woods questioned whether the Government had reconsidered alternatives to liquefied natural gas (LNG) amid elevated prices and the Middle East crisis. Brown said options had been considered and the Government’s procurement process would take current conditions into account, while arguing that solar would not resolve the dry-winter supply challenge.

keyExchanges.speaker: Scott Willis (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Is he aware that 200,000 households were not able to keep their homes adequately warm in 2025, and, if so, what concrete actions has he taken that will reduce power bills this winter?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National, Minister for Energy)
keyExchanges.quote: We are seeing good signs in the energy market, and that will have a positive impact for consumers.

topicSummaries.topic: Labour Challenges Government on Jobs and Pay Equity
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes in employment and pay equity affect household incomes and opportunities for workers, including young people and women.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ginny Andersen challenged Economic Growth Minister Nicola Willis to defend the Government’s claim that it was helping jobseekers, citing fewer young people, women and manufacturing workers in employment than two years earlier. Andersen also linked the dispute to the repeal of pay equity legislation and the end of work on 23 active claims. Willis said the Government was improving conditions for businesses to invest and hire, pointing to planning and employment-law changes, investment incentives and energy supply; she also said a funded pay equity regime remained in place. The exchange featured competing accounts of the Government’s economic record, rather than a new employment initiative.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can she claim that when there are 14,600 fewer women in work compared to two years ago and her Government has repealed pay equity legislation, which undid the work of 23 active claims?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National, Minister for Economic Growth)
keyExchanges.quote: Because we still have in place a very workable pay equity regime, which is fully funded.

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Transport Governance Overhaul Passes Third Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes shift key local transport decisions to elected Auckland representatives and may affect planning, public transport and neighbourhood roads.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament passed the Local Government (Auckland Council) (Transport Governance) Amendment Bill at its final reading. It moves most local transport planning, policy and delivery functions from Auckland Transport to Auckland Council, gives local boards authority over specified local-road decisions, and reshapes Auckland Transport to focus on public transport. A joint Government–council Auckland Regional Transport Committee will develop a long-term transport plan, including a 30-year plan, and the transition is expected to take six months. Labour and the Greens supported the bill while raising concerns about funding, local representation and the committee’s appointments; Te Pāti Māori supported it but said Māori representation and the protection of Māori interests were not sufficiently guaranteed. ACT supported the bill while questioning the role of Māori participation in plan design.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: My main critique of this bill—though we are supporting it—and I think one thing that we’re going to have to watch very closely is the representation of the regional transport committee.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Court (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: ACT supports the Local Government (Auckland Council) (Transport Governance) Amendment Bill. It’s a great bill and restores, for the first time, the ability of Auckland to take control of its regional planning and link that up—where the city expects growth to occur with where it intends to fund infrastructure.

topicSummaries.topic: Peters Defends New Zealand’s Position on Iran Strikes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The Government’s position on military action abroad can affect New Zealand’s diplomacy, legal obligations and exposure to international tensions and associated costs.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Vanushi Walters pressed Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters on the Government’s position regarding US and Israeli strikes on Iran, including whether the Prime Minister had sought an explicit public endorsement and whether legal advice had been obtained. Peters said the Government’s 1 March statement remained its position, that New Zealand was not participating in the conflict, and that it supported de-escalation and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. He described foreign policy as his responsibility, exercised in consultation with the Prime Minister and others, but did not directly clarify whether the Prime Minister had requested a change in public position. The Speaker declined Walters’ request for an urgent debate, saying the matter did not warrant setting aside the House’s scheduled business.

keyExchanges.speaker: Vanushi Walters (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Who is the final decision maker on New Zealand’s foreign policy: the Minister of Foreign Affairs or the Prime Minister?

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (NZ First, Minister of Foreign Affairs)
keyExchanges.quote: The Minister of Foreign Affairs is charged with that responsibility but in consultation with the Prime Minister, obviously; the ministerial contacts, as well; and other MPs, including sometimes crossing the House to make sure that there is a unified view in this country.

topicSummaries.topic: Workplace Safety Reforms Draw Questions Over Worker Protections
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The rules determine which workplace hazards employers must manage and may affect workers’ safety as well as business and ACC costs.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Teanau Tuiono questioned Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden about reforms that he said would remove duties to manage psychological and musculoskeletal risks for most businesses, and asked whether ACC levies could rise. Van Velden said the reforms would focus employers on critical risks and reduce paper-based compliance, while maintaining duties for psychosocial risks likely to cause serious harm. She did not give a direct guarantee about future ACC levies, saying she was not responsible for ACC, but added that officials expected cost reductions. The Speaker noted that the Minister’s lengthy answer had not directly addressed the levy question.

keyExchanges.speaker: Teanau Tuiono (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Why is she removing the duty to manage work-related stress and other psychological harms from 97 percent of businesses when these are the second biggest cause of work-related harm and, according to WorkSafe, the cause of 40 work-related suicides a year?

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT, Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety)
keyExchanges.quote: I am not excluding psychosocial risk. If a psychosocial risk is likely to result in a death, notifiable injury, illness, or incident, then it must be managed as a critical risk.

topicSummaries.topic: Serious Fraud Office Bill Advances With Safeguards Under Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill could expand investigators’ ability to obtain digital evidence in complex fraud cases, while raising questions about privacy and the limits on enforcement powers.
topicSummaries.content: The Serious Fraud Office Amendment Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Justice Committee, with a report due by 31 August 2026. The Government said the 1990 law needs updating to cover digital evidence, faster warrant applications and the practical management of search sites, and to align evidence admissibility rules with the Evidence Act 2006. Labour, the Greens and other parties supported further examination, but speakers raised concerns about safeguards after a Court of Appeal case criticised the SFO’s use of warrants. Labour also questioned whether the agency had enough resources to carry out its work, while the Government argued that modern powers were needed to pursue serious fraud and corruption.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mark Mitchell (National, Minister of Police)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill gives the SFO the powers it needs to investigate and prosecute serious fraud and corruption in the digital age.

keyExchanges.speaker: Duncan Webb (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We do want to make sure that it isn’t just giving them more powers, because they haven’t got enough money.

topicSummaries.topic: Anti-Money-Laundering Bills Reach Final Debate, But Vote Is Pending
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes would reduce some compliance duties for lower-risk activity and reorganise oversight of rules intended to detect money laundering and terrorist financing.
topicSummaries.content: Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee moved the third reading of two anti-money-laundering and countering-financing-of-terrorism bills, proposing a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs to replace the Reserve Bank, Financial Markets Authority and DIA arrangement. The Government said the reforms would reduce unnecessary compliance for lower-risk activity, focus enforcement on serious threats and introduce an industry levy as part of a hybrid funding model. Labour and the Greens supported the bills but called for effective safeguards, adequate investigative expertise and careful scrutiny of the levy and of risks involving newer financial instruments. The debate was interrupted at adjournment and set down for resumption at the next sitting; no third-reading vote was recorded that day.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicole McKee (ACT, Associate Minister of Justice)
keyExchanges.quote: These bills create a genuinely risk-based approach that directs effort where it is needed most.

keyExchanges.speaker: Duncan Webb (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We support this bill, but these bills largely lower the bar in terms of obligations.

topicSummaries.topic: Cancer Infusion Services to Expand Across 28 Sites
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: More treatment capacity closer to home could reduce travel burdens and help patients access cancer infusions sooner.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown outlined a nationwide expansion of community cancer infusion services, with 14 new centres and 14 existing sites to be expanded. The Government expects about 13,000 additional infusions in 2025–26, a 12 percent increase on prior volumes, and says the completed expansion will provide 218 additional chair days of treatment space each week. Brown said the extra capacity is intended to support access to 33 cancer treatments funded through a $604 million medicines investment and reduce patients’ need to travel long distances. The programme is being rolled out across regions, with some centres already open and further locations planned.

keyExchanges.speaker: Vanessa Weenink (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Why is expanding infusion capacity important?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National, Minister of Health)
keyExchanges.quote: This will allow hundreds more patients to be treated weekly across the country, with each chair typically used by three to five patients per day, ensuring patients can get access to treatments when they need them, without unnecessary delays, and closer to home.

conclusion: The day delivered a concrete change to Auckland transport governance, but debate over household costs, public safeguards and the balance between regulation and enforcement remained unresolved.
